review:
When I first started using a PC for gaming, all I had was a little PC that my dad had built for me and my sister to do schoolwork on. We had limited access to the internet at the time, so on a rare occasion when we did, I went looking around for games to play. I poked around on Gamejolt, and ran into a little FPS that promised a multiplayer-esque experience in a single player game. The graphics were primitive, so I was sure it could run on our computer, and best of all I didn't need to be online to play it.

That game was a very old alpha of Ravenfield. It had strange AI, two maps, and a handful of guns to choose from. It was the first FPS I ever played with a mouse and keyboard (save for one time I played Red Eclipse and Assault Cube on my uncle's laptop), and I played it for countless hours.

Some years later, I learned that Ravenfield had advanced far beyond what I had been playing. I eventually bought my own gaming laptop, and the first thing I did was install Steam and buy Ravenfield, to see what it had become.

Ravenfield is an entirely single player game that strives to behave like a multiplayer game. Rather than play through a series of levels in a campaign, Ravenfield places you onto wide, open map with with two teams of AI controlled players in a multiplayer-style game mode. This, on paper, sounds quite odd. Usually, bots are included in an FPS as an afterthought for when you don't have anyone else to play with. But in Ravenfield, playing against bots is the entire game. This, as it turns out, works amazingly well for a whole variety of reasons, and serves to create a very unique experience:

A: You can have as many (or as few) players as you want, and balance the teams however you want. If you so desire, you can have battles bigger than you could ordinarily achieve with real humans. The only limit is the strength of your computer.

B: There is no pressure to take things seriously. This, combined with the sandbox nature of the game, can lead to a lot of fun. You want to grab a helicopter and attempt to use it just to kamikaze one individual enemy? No reason you can't. The AI aren't going to get mad at you for wasting resources, (and vehicles respawn quite quickly, so they are quite expendable). No matter how you play, neither you nor the AI have any reason to get upset.

Now, this alone will get old eventually, so going into playing this game, I HIGHLY recommend that you download lots and lots of mods. The single best thing about this game is the huge modding community around it. Is there a real world (or even fictional) gun you like? Nine times out of ten you can find a decent mod for it. The workshop is also full of cool or ridiculous skins, maps, vehicles, and even mutators. All of these things combined, plus the ability to create and save presets, means Ravenfield can be almost anything you want it to be. This is the true experience of Ravenfield. Not the vanilla experience, but the experience of going from fighting in WWII, to fighting in modern times, to fighting a futuristic laser battle, to just applying random mutators to make the most cursed game possible. I've spent hours just downloading huge batches of weapons, and then meticulously balance testing them all against each other one after another. How many other games can you name where armies of Freddy Mercury and the Engineer engage each other in trench warfare with Fallout guns and A-10 Warthogs? Put simply, if your game doesn't take ten minutes to load, you're not playing Ravenfield to its fullest.

I've barely scratched the surface of this game. The rest is something you need to experience for yourself. For what you get, 15 dollars is an absolute burglary. To start you out though, I recommend that you download the entire World War II Collection by mellamomellamo, the NERF Pack by New_BEING_Newbie, and Project Eagle by Eagle Pancake (Also make sure you get lots of maps and some skins). This barely touches on all of the great mods that you should play, but discovering stuff for yourself while browsing the workshop is part of the fun.

That's all I have to say. I hope I managed to get at least one person to cough up the 15 bucks for this game, it really is worth it.

The real appeal of this game is in the mods. On its own, this game is a super bare bones, basic, vanilla PvE, Red vs Blue FPS with low-res poly graphics, basic levels, short list of simple game modes, and your standard-fare spread of weapons. But there is a whole community of people in the workshop section who have collectively produced THOUSANDS of mods. 99% of them are extremely quick to download and even easier to implement in-game. From things as simple as changing character skins and giving your gun a basic "+" cross hair when hip firing, all the way to flawless recreations of every Titanfall gun, advanced movement mods, map packs recreating levels from your favorite games, and so much more. 

For example, I just played a 25 (SWAT) vs 25 (Storm Troopers) match on the Battlefront, Tantive map. The weapon pool consisted of every Star Wars, Apex Legends, and Titanfall 2 weapon. I ran a R-99/Wingman combo the whole time, which, by the way, were recreated immaculately, right down to the reload sounds and animations. The match was set to 1.5x movement speed with dashing and crouch-sliding enabled, and enemy AI cranked up to elite difficulty. 

Better still, even with all the mods, the game is very friendly to lower-end PCs. 

Worth every penny at full price. If it's on sale and you STILL don't buy it, I'll find where you live.

I stumbled upon this game looking through a game queue, and I am glad that I have. If you like shooters with no nonsense, this is the game for you!

The thing that stood out the most when going into my first battle was the simplicity of the game. There is no gaining levels, no buying weapons, and no attachments. (According to Steelraven7 - the sole developer, this was to keep the weapons being used for what they are meant for). You hop in and enjoy. You (and your computer) are the limit, not the game. The excitement you get at the beginning of the match is based off of the experience of the game, and not the next thing you are trying to unlock.

Another highlight of the game that I noticed later, when the two teams met up at a point to fight, was the use of physics. When a soldier is injured enough or is within the blast radius of a ballistic weapon, he will fall over or be sent hurdling 30 feet into the air. When vehicles wreck, they don't just break. They explode. Personnel carriers will be blown sky high and lose their wheels when they run out of HP. Helicopters and planes will hilariously flail around in the air before exploding after making contact with the ground. Sea vehicles explode and sink. The occupants of these vehicles will also be sent flopping through the air and/or on the ground with the game's rag doll physics.

The aforementioned aspect of no levels is another important piece of the game. The progress of the game is based off of your ability, rather than the equipment that you unlock. The game will let you decide how to progress, rather than take away equipment until you are "good enough to handle it." To challenge yourself you can change the game's difficulty settings instead of drag yourself up the ladder of ranks that most games make you do.

Ravenfield is a stark contrast to most other well known contemporary shooters. While those games try to make the game feel like a movie where you are the main character, this game lets you do and feel how you want, yet you are not the center of the experience. You can fight alongside your fellow blue or red soldiers, you can take to the skies with planes and dominate the air, you can use a helicopter to tease the enemies defenses, you can bulldoze your way through enemy infantry with a tank, or you can group up with a few soldiers and hop in a personnel carrier, all while being able to go wherever you choose on the map. There are no invisible walls, or voids, and the game is not limited to paths or buildings. The game is pure freedom.

The developer keeps things interesting with frequent updates. With each update there is always at least one big change. When Beta 6 came out, the character models were changed from block characters to low-poly soldiers. An in-dev version of the most popular map, Archipelago, was also added. A temple map was also added.

However, being a game in very early development, it has some problems that will need fixing in the future. The AI can be hit and miss sometimes. For instance, leaving the aircraft carrier on the Archipelago map. If you spawn many soldiers, they will crowd the dock part of the aircraft carriers to get into small boats. They do not have problems getting into the boats, but they do have issues driving the boats out of the ship. In this phenomenon, boats fill run into one another and become piled up like a stack of pancakes. AIs that are in land vehicles never fail to flatten you if you are within 20 feet of the spawn area. They do not look where they are going yet. They will always try to shoot you from across the map if they have seen you, even if there are more important things to shoot. This can be seen as funny for some players, or frustrating for others. The game also lacks a large amount of maps. Of course, the game will be updated to have more in the near future. The maps you get are good, but there only a few unique maps at the moment. As of right now though, you can download maps from other users or make maps for yourself with the map making tools if you are not satisfied by these maps.

All in all, Ravenfield is unique, but also reminds me of simpler games. The game is a refreshing break from the grinding involved in many modern games. If you enjoyed the days when games were simple freedom, I guarantee you will like this game.

Man where to start. This is probably going to be a TL;DR for people but I'll say what needs to be said. This was the first game i got since switching from Console to PC and its my top 2 played game for a reason, a good reason. This game is a sandbox warfare dream. You control who is on the battlefield and become a lowly soldier. You're not a super man, one shot to the face and you're gone just like any other. It isnt the realism or the graphics, this game offers raw fun, alongside its bountyful mods which span from guns to maps, more and more. if you have the money lying around for it, this game is a go getter for those who can look past graphics and the fact that this is singleplayer. Thank you steelraven and the community for making this game awesome!

By itself, it's the most fun you can have with bots.

TONS of mods too, with the Workshop you can customize this game as much as you want. Transform the game into WW2 or Star Wars, replace the arsenal with Nerf guns, add more vehicles and guns, toss memes and jokes into the game, etc. I've become addicted to modding the game!

Positives:
- Great gameplay, similar to Battlefield wherein you capture objectives on the map and grind your enemy's numbers down.
- A big arsenal of weapons that feel good to use. Guns have notable recoil and bullets are real projectiles, not hitscans, so landing shots at a distance takes some skill and feels rewarding.
- Goofy ragdoll physics when you get hit by an explosion or nail an enemy with a high caliber weapon.
- Competent AI that can form its own squads, capture objectives, operate vehicles, and generally pose a threat to you.
- Runs great on average hardware, even with extra bots added.
- A somewhat basic but functional system to issue commands to your army. You can also form a squad once in combat and order your troops around. 

Negatives:
- Some gun sounds are mediocre
- Some minor glitches like the one guided missile launcher in the game not working consistently, some weapons not having a reload sound, these are things the dev can fix though.
- No in-game tutorial, some game modes or vehicle functions could use explaining, but it's not too hard to figure out.
- NO MULTIPLAYER, and the Dev has stated he will not add it, although this does not bother me at all personally. If you are looking for multiplayer this is not your game.

Great game with an interesting concept, very fun to play every now and then. It's a low poly first person shooter with plenty of weapon and vehicular options with interesting and engaging maps.

PROS:
-MODS!! yes, this is perhaps the best part of the game, the community is amazing providing with plenty of mods and weapon packs to fully flesh out the game. There is a mod for anything and everything, from WW1 to WW2 to modern weapons and maps, even Star Wars! Lots available and lots more to come!!
-Regular Updates: SteelRaven7, the developer, is always engaged with the community listening and responding to feedback, and updating the game every other week adding new content and mechanics. To get into this it's best to join the Discord server
-Sandbox style game: You can pretty much set up games how you want, how many bots, how many on each team, what weapons they carry, how they attack/defend etc... it gives you great control on how the battle plays out
-Well optimised: The game runs very well, even on my potato PC (Some maps may be laggy, just lower the res)
-Quick and fun: A great plus for me. You don't need to put hours into the game, as you can simply start the game play a match and exit, Maps load fast (Modded maps may take time to load) making it great to just chill out in a 30 minute break.
-Vehicles and weapons: Really great selection of all sorts of vehicles and weapons, with SteelRaven adding more every now and then. It really make it feel like a Battlefield style game with tanks, helicopters and planes all zooming by.

CONS:
-MULTIPLAYER!: Yes this game is SINGLE PLAYER and will remain so, as SteelRaven7 has expresed his desire for this game to be purely single player. It's not a big deal for me and I don't mind it, but I am aware that a lot of people are very disappointed in this factor, and it turns them away from the game
-Lacking AI: Sometimes the AI can be rather lacking in the brains department, but it is improving with each update. Some bots may ignore orders and run into the slaughter or simply just do stupid AI things
-Bugs and glitches: Yes the game is still in Early Access, so do expect some unusual stuff to happen, there are a couple of known bugs and glitches which the dev is working on, some are new and fun to point out in the Discord

Wow I have a lot to say about this game. I mean, there is a LOT of potential here. It's almost like the perfect early access game: There is enough there to keep you interested for now, it is continually supported and updated with new and exciting content, and there are so many different paths it can go down. However, note how I said *almost* perfect, because yeah, this game has some flaws. But we'll get to that, first let's see what makes this game good.

[h1] The Good [/h1]

This game perfectly fits a cool little subgenre of a "combat-sandbox", where you design combat scenarios and you get to fight in said scenario. This is only compounded by it's amazing integration with the steam workshop, the quality of mods for this game are through the roof with weapons, maps, vehicles, and even more things with the recently added "mutators". However even without mods, this game already has great weapon, gamemode, and map variety, although I would still definitely recommend you check out some mods. The AI is, for the most part, pretty good, especially in the new Spec Ops mode. Not the best AI I have seen in a game, but I'll get to that later. For the most part the AI does fit the "combat-sandbox" I touched on earlier. The gunplay is solid, the vehicles are pretty nice for the most part, and the ways that the player is able to move fits the game pretty well. Because of the more sandbox nature of this game, I find it is really re-playable as well. However it isn't all roses, this game does have problems.

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

It feels like some of the games systems have at least one thing to them that peeves me just a little bit. For example, while the guns are fun to use, by default there is no crosshair, and you kind of are forced to aim down sights. I know there is a mutator for that now, but still, for the longest time there was absolutely no way to get that, and as somebody who plays a ton of classic fps this bugs me to no end. Also, the AI really isn't perfect. There isn't much too the AI in truth (unless you are playing the spec ops mode) and ordering the AI around can be... tough at times. Also, if you take damage there is a chance to get knocked down. Sometimes this can be a life savior, but other times it can be super frustrating, as it can act as a pseudo-stun lock of sorts, where you are doomed to fall down, get up, fall down again, rinse and repeat until you die. Vehicles also have some slight annoyances to them, especially the planes and the quad. The quad gets flipped WAY too easily, and the sensitivity of the planes is all out of wack. However, these are not my biggest gripes with it.

[h1] The Ugly [/h1]

I only have a small number of things to put into this category, but these are still some major things. Firstly, this game can have some pretty bad glitches. Surprisingly, they don't happen that often, but it still sucks when one occurs. I have fallen through the map and not died, my character has turned into spaghetti, and the ui of the game's campaign mode has straight up disappeared on me. This doesn't happen often, but when it does, I have to shut off the game in order to calm myself down. It's super infuriating. Sometimes the AI is completely broken as well, and while this also doesn't happen often, it's infuriating when either the AI randomly turns into a super soldier, or becomes completely incompetent. That's pretty much it for the ugly though.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

I like to think of this game as the quintessential early access game. It's got clear flaws, but it's future is super promising. I would say that you should definitely get this game if you enjoy experiences like Garry's mod, where you can create your own scenarios, and also are a fan of a modern military/realistic style of FPS. Before I end this review, however, I would like to state some things I'd like to see added or fixed. I would definitely like to see an option to disable getting knocked down. I'd also like to see the AI more fleshed out. Maybe make some less open maps so that we can see AI that acts more like AI enemies in games like F.E.A.R., Half Life 1, or other games with clever AI (but still AI that has clear weaknesses). Just fleshing out the AI more in general would be great. For my final score, I'm giving Ravenfield in it's early access stat (as of November 11, 2020) a 7/10.

I just wanted to finally write a review and hope SteelRaven sees it. I think you're the man. I've spent not hours, not days, not even weeks, but months at this point enjoying your fine game. I didn't check the box saying I got this game for free, but technically I guess I did.

To give you some context to this review, my family is by no means wealthy. Christmas was always a wonderful event every year, but our gifts to each other normally aren't very grandiose. It was around a decade ago that my dad got me some PC gaming magazine in my stocking with one of those free demo CDs attached. It contained a bunch of alpha or beta indie games and applications. To date, that disc is one of the coolest gifts I've ever gotten. Best twenty bucks my dad ever spent. 

I still have that disk, and I've had to get it cleaned on one of those CD-buffing machines like 3 times at my local used game store to remove the scratches from its years of use. They look at me like I'm nuts every time I bring it in. They think I'm crazy for constantly refurbishing a demo disc from an old magazine, but it's irreplaceable.

It had some great games on it, but my favorite was this battlefield-like FPS with these silly little square guys. I loved it. I played for hours on end, and I was amazed by the ragdoll physics, the helicopters, the feel of the guns, the awesome maps. I'm normally one to rage at games when I lose and die, but for some reason, I never did with this one. I loved watching my little block dude roll down a hill looking like he was getting his belly tickled when he got blown up. I laughed my ass off every time I got shot in the crotch, or blown up by a rocket by a surprisingly sophisticated AI.

Ravenfield isn't a shitty, cheap, exploitable COD game, nor is it an overly expensive Battlefield game that demands I purchase an $80 "Season Pass". It's no half-assed $20 DLC so the AAA investor "developers" can afford to hire more cheap furry prostitutes to tickle their nether regions and fan them with palm fronds. It's just a fun game made by, I imagine, a very cool guy.

So fast forward a few years and I'm 30 now. I have a good job, and some spending money for the very first time in my life. I finally purchase my own gaming laptop with the entirety of my first decent paycheck ever. I have it custom made by a guy in town who builds PCs, and I spare no expense. He assures me it can play a heavily-modded Skyrim with ease.

So, naturally the first thing I do upon downloading Steam is go on a search to find my little Ravenfield demo game that I've been religiously playing on an old Toshiba from the 2000's.

What I found astonished me. The song "A Whole New World" from Aladdin blared in my imagination as I scrolled, wide-eyed, through what I found. Not only was this SteelRaven fellow still working on his awesome game, there was a community of modders adding absolutely anything and everything imaginable to my favorite FPS.

Now this is the only game I play. I check the workshop daily for the amazing new stuff people create. Firing up this now heavily-modded masterpiece takes about twenty minutes, and makes my PC wail like a steam locomotive. Even my dad, who started it all, sees this and thinks I'm an idiot.

I can't believe we started with block bois fighting over a grassy island with small arms. After posting this review, I'm going to reenact the American Civil War's Battle of Bull Run, except the Union Army is now made up of British SAS Paratroopers with SAW LMGs and F-35 jets.

Thank you, SteelRaven. I love this game so god-damned much, and I love you.

[b]It doesn't take long in-game to get the appeal of [i]Ravenfield[/i][/b]. It's a simple concept of military sandbox shooter, yet executed in a way that nearly anyone who mildly enjoys FPS titles would find engaging and addictive. 

[i]Essentially, there is a military battle occuring on medium-to-small scale prebuilt maps.[/i] It is only you and bots; there is no multiplayer what-so-ever. The landscape is dotted with 'zones' or 'bases' that you can capture and control, which then act as spawn points for whenever you are (frequently) killed. There are several cool vehicles that you can use seemlessly. The airplanes and helicopters take a quick bit of skill to operate, which is neat. 

You only control one soldier at a time (FPS-style), and as far as I can tell you can't give orders or anything like that. This is a run-and-gun affair. [b]The only strategy that matters is the one [i]you[/i] bring to the table.[/b] There is a map you can consult in real-time that shows the battle unfolding, and helps you develope your approach. The guns are standard military affair, and all feel different and lend different strategies. 

[b]This is one of those titles that looked 'meh' to me in videos, but when I played it - I got it.[/b] Being a sandboxy type of game, your mileage will vary in how much fun you get out of it. There are not currently any missions or 'story mode' (apparently planned), so you have to enjoy simply going for the thrill of the win at this point in time.

[b]Pros:[/b]
+Really engaging warfare on the FPS scale
+AI units 'feel' and 'act' real and give this game legs to stand on
+To me, 'single player only' is a good thing for SOME GAMES, and it works well here - so bravo for that
+Graphics are clean and work well for this game; the performance seems great and I bet this can run on a toaster
+Addicting gameplay that also offers some depth and strategic variation
+Guns are all fun and play differently
+Vehicles such as tanks, ATVs, helicopters, airplanes, boats, etc. that you can seemlessly operate
+Slow motion mode
+Battle customiaztion options; if you want (and your computer can handle it) hundreds of soldiers and mass chaos, great, or you can have just a few soldiers and much more strategy going on
+This title has been in developement for a long time which gives me hope that chance of abandonment is low and there is a long bright future of work that will be done
+Steam Workshop support is coming

[b]Cons:[/b]
-Yes, there are rough edges at this point in time
-No music (which is kind of neat and makes the warfare feel more 'real', but it would be something I'd like to see in the future)
-Controller support is here, but you still need the mouse for the menus - and really, you should probably think twice before buying this with the intent of controller only at this point (just my experience)

[b][i]Ravenfield[/i] is an ordinary concept executed extraordinarily well.[/b] Well worth full price if this is your kind of jam.

Pros
+ Solid gameplay through and through. Guns use actual projectiles instead of hitscan, so there's more skill involved in aiming. The AI on both sides is surprisingly competent. There's really not much more to say. It plays like Battlefield or Battlefront.
+ Mod friendliness (including an in-game map editor) provides for both a dedicated community of creators and a theoretically endless amount of ways to customize the game.
+ Ragdoll physics and a few glitches here and there provide for much hilarity.
+ The minimalist graphics mean there's a relatively low entry point as far as your hardware is concerned. They still look nice and give the game it's unique charm. You can also customize the number of bots to scale the game according to your whim.

Cons
- While I don't really view it as a big deal, you should be aware that this game is singleplayer only. There's no online, LAN, or splitscreen currently available.

Verdict
If you're like me and you grew up playing Star Wars Battlefront (the old ones) Instant Action on single player, this game will be a serious nostalgia trip. Even if you didn't, there's hours of fun to be had fighting across the Ravenfield and browsing the Workshop. Suck it, Red!

Ever played with toy soldiers or Legos growing up, staging massive battles with anachronistic weapons and random locations? Ravenfield could be considered a videogame adaption of that concept. It's a low-polygon singleplayer first-person shooter that pits two teams of bots against each other on huge battlefields, and throws you into the action on one side or the other. The game sacrifices graphical detail for scale, as you can set dozens or even hundreds of bots against each other. 

Ravenfield's gameplay is similar to Battlefield 2's. You spawn on an outpost, choose your loadout, and work with teammates to secure points on the map for your team. Instead of a class system, you can choose a primary weapon, a secondary, and three pieces of equipment. Some items, like rocket launchers, take up two spaces of equipment. Vehicles are scattered around most maps, like jeeps, helicopters, and bombers. All of these features give battles different fronts and dimensions - you can see combat in the air, on the ground, or at sea. These approaches can overlap, meaning that helicopters can battle gunboats while tanks attack them from the shore. It gets crazy in an entertaining way.

The battlefields in Ravenfield are like sandboxes that you can adjust to your liking. You can disable vehicles, limit AI weapons, and swap between times of day. Sliders like team balance and map control allow you to tweak advantages for both sides. Respawn times can be fine-tuned to your liking, but having it too slow or too fast can unbalance maps.

There are several modes you can choose from. Battalions is like Battlefield's conquest mode, where you battle for outposts and try to eliminate the other team's reinforcements. Point Match is a variant of it, where you instead try to get 300 points more than the enemy team while holding outposts. Spec Ops is a Far Cry-like mode where you sneak around the map and complete objectives (destroy vehicles, kill certain enemies, blow up ammo crates, etc.) alongside some bots. Rounding out the list is Haunted, a survival mode where you and a few other bots hold out against a skeleton army.

The highlight of Ravenfield is the modding support. The game has a fantastic modding community that puts out high-quality content. The workshop features custom weapons, maps, and vehicles that all compliment each other. Muskets and flintlock pistols? Laser guns? Maps set in muddy trenches or seaside villas? All of these are available alongside so many other options. The low-detail nature of the game also means that the mods have smaller file sizes, which makes downloading them less of a burden.

Ravenfield has really shaped up since the start of its early access release. Its clunkier mechanics have been improved, and its support for custom content has increased even further. The development of Ravenfield shows that not all Early Access games turn out to be busts, and that developers can live up to the promises they made. Frankly, it should be a model for other Early Access games to follow.

In my opinion, Ravenfield would benefit from adding these improvements before release:
[list]
[*]Allowing AI to use akimbo weapons.
[*][strike]A scoreboard at the end of matches that shows your overall stats.[/strike] As of July 6th 2018, a scoreboard for the player and bots has been added. It can be accessed by pressing Tab.
[*][strike]Giving Biplanes immunity to homing missiles or greater defense.[/strike] As of Feb 1st 2018, you can now replace Biplanes with custom vehicles, giving that vehicle slot more utility.
[*][strike]The option to limit your available weapons. You can currently only restrict AI weapons. It would make the weapon selection menu easier to navigate when you have mods installed.[/strike] As of Oct 6th 2018, you can toggle an option to limit yourself to the AI's weapons.
[*][strike]At least two or more official maps to round out the list. An urban map or jungle map would be ideal.[/strike] Several new maps have been added to the game since its release, providing more variety alongside the workshop's collection of custom maps.

[*]A tutorial for flying helicopters and bombers.

As it stands now, I enjoy Ravenfield. It has great potential, and I think the developer is worth putting one's confidence in. He has made something truly unique here.

Ravenfield is built for people that like the large-scale, objective-based skirmishes of the Battlefield games, but also don't like playing with other people in general. Ravenfield is botmatch heaven in a lightweight package, designed for those of us that enjoy those silly and frantic moments that only subpar AI can deliver.

The game has super low system requirements, due to its lack of things like dynamic lighting, high-poly models, or fancy post-processing. This is definitely an intentional move, however; Ravenfield features large sprawling maps and a potentially huge number of combatants (you can set this number to whatever you want; one-on-one or literally hundreds of soldiers on the battlefield). You'll find your traditional Battlefield gameplay here; the main gametypes see you capturing spawn points or reducing your enemy's respawn tickets to 0. Weapons are loosely categorized into classes, but on the loadout screen you are free to mix and match as you see fit. The game features a health system, Battlefield-style vehicles, and a rudimentary squad system. All of this comes together with you as the sole human player in a sea of friendly and hostile AI soldiers that boast the perfect amount of pure stupidity. In smaller matches, you're usually going to win because your actions so strongly influence the tide of battle, but the game really shines when there's 100 people on each side and you're frantically battling over a new spawn point while your stupid teammates hand another one over to the enemy. These kinds of botmatches are fun in their own right...they're certainly not for everybody, but if botmatches are your thing, there's plenty of fun to be had here. While the game's official content is a little limited right now, more maps will certainly be added as development continues. And with Steam Workshop being introduced to the game, there's plenty of user-created maps and weapons to fill that void. This whole game is being developed by just one guy, and for being a one-man show it's a really impressive piece of work.

If you're more of a multiplayer person, you'll probably be disappointed here. But if you like botmatches and you just like killing time by shooting at things in a nice little sandbox-y package, you'll probably end up sinking a decent amount of time into Ravenfield. Pick it up if you're someone like me, looking for a multiplayer experience in a singleplayer package.

[h1]Overview[/h1]

Ravenfield can best be described as an offline Battlefield. Despite the wide open areas and literally as many bots as your computer can handle, you are completely alone in Ravenfield. Just you and your AI buddies, fighting over whatever objective you've set for yourself or just having a out-and-out deathmatch.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

In simple terms, Ravenfield is a simple FPS. In more ways than one; you may have noticed the graphics sort of invoke a kind of toy soldier feel with low polygons and vibrant bright colors, which also handily makes it easier to handle higher bot counts.

What Ravenfield [i]offers[/i] is a sense of battlefield-like scale (or bigger), with bots that are mildly competent at killing you. It's actually quite impressive be attacking a town and see two planes having a legitimate dogfight overhead, or tanks dueling in a pass. It's kind of Planetside 2 in that way, but with no humans involved. Just you, putting yourself in the center of the spectacle. 

It's a kind of game you just screw around in; I've yet to actually ever complete a 'round' in the game, but still get a lot of kick from just jumping into firefights and see how long I can last. The game's really active modding scene also adds to this, just furthering its replay value.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

For the price, I think it's worth your money. It's a neat sandbox shooter, with nearly endless versatility.

What sets this game apart from a game like Battlefield is its ragdoll mechanics. You see, it is actually a crucial element for weapon balance in Ravenfield. It allows certain weapons to feel more powerful, without them being instant kill. For example, the amphibious vehicle with its auto gun can only instant kill with a direct hit, but its splash damage will keep infantry falling over, allowing your allies to get an easy kill, or prepare them to be finished off with direct hits. Another big example of this is with shotguns. While the kill range is similar to somewhere between Halo CE and Halo 2 shotguns, it can knock infantry over into a ragdoll at medium range, allowing you to close the distance.

I appreciate this admittedly atypical method of weapon balance, since most of the time the bigger AAA games would simply buff or nerf numbers, which really never satisfy everyone, and often a weapon would simply be abandoned by the community if it got nerfed too hard. I fail to see this happening in this game, where the ragdoll physics aren't there just for fun, but are an integral part of the gameplay.

Other uses for the ragdoll in this sandbox is help give a player a second chance if they run into a bad situation. Enough simultaneous damage will turn your character into a ragdoll, and thus makes your hit box a lot harder to hit; though you are helpless to get up for a second or two. When you start to get up, you can immediately start moving to cover even before you can start shooting. The same thing happens with sniper hits. Headshots are still headshots however, and the ragdoll will not save you every time, and you should make sure to double-tap enemies who may have simply been knocked into a ragdoll state.

The last thing I want to mention is the omni-directional sprinting. In a game like Arma, normally looking around while sprinting would be dedicated to a separate key. In this game, you can just do so naturally with no fuss. However, what prevents you from sprinting everywhere all the time is the fact you are more likely to ragdoll if shot; though the same goes for enemies sprinting at you. Shoot them in the legs, and they'll face-plant! Between how the ragdoll and sprinting mechanics work, this allows for either methodical or twitchy gameplay styles to coexist, each equally viable.

You can set what both factions are called, set their colour, even have them use custom names simply by editing a notepad document. With the recent update the UI has become much more convenient and easier to navigate along with rarity configuration. The game lets you assign any weapon and vehicle you want to any faction. You want to turn an an entire map into a tank warfare zone; Assigning every vehicle slot with tanks. Or a medieval warfare with catapults, swords, crossbows? Workshop offers all the toys you want. There is no limit. Seriously, the workshop support for this game is super vast. The game is a love letter to any mod user. It allows you to mod every detail from maps, vehicle models, physics to graphics, sounds, AI, and more. The community is super helpful too should you decide to make your own mutator (mods that change game mechanics). This is basically what a game becomes when it is made with pure love and passion. Bless SteelRaven7 and the Ravenfield community

Ravenfield is a modular, customizable, all-engrossing military sandbox. One driven by its expansive and active modding community. A modding community that, frankly, makes this game worthwhile. 

At its core, this game is a FPS with bots. How many bots? As many as your hardware can handle. What time period? Depends on what mods you've downloaded. You can even create or download maps to duke it out on. 

My favorite set-up is to play as U.S. SWAT troops with standard American weaponry while battling 40K Mechanicus wielding deadly Imperium weaponry. These battles can range from small European towns to the beaches of Normandy. 

I highly recommend this game for anyone looking to mess around in a low-stakes game.
